## Export Compliance Procedure: [Company], US SaaS

**Version** 1.0 · **Effective** [date] · **Owner** Export Compliance Lead · Rules cited as of October 2026. Verify each one against the primary source before you adopt this.

> I'm not a lawyer or your empowered official. Have export-control counsel review this before you adopt it.

**1. Scope.** This applies to all employees and contractors. It covers every sign-up, sale, renewal, download (desktop and mobile apps, SDKs, CLIs), release of source code or technical data, and support interaction. US export controls (EAR, 15 CFR Parts 730–774) and OFAC sanctions (31 CFR Chapter V) cover services and payments as well as shipments.

**2. Roles.**
- **Export Compliance Lead** (a named person, plus a backup): owns this procedure, can stop any deal, account or release, and is the only person who can release a hold.
- **Sales, Support, Finance, Engineering, People:** follow these steps and escalate red flags the same day.
- **Export-control counsel:** handles licenses, classification requests, voluntary disclosures and anything that looks like a violation.

**3. Classify what we offer.** Keep a dated worksheet for the platform, each downloadable client and our source code. It records the encryption functions, mass-market status (likely 5A992/5D992; verify 15 CFR 740.17 and 742.15) and any self-classification report due. BIS advisory opinions have generally not treated remote SaaS access as an export of our software. Downloads, on-prem installs and code releases are exports, though, and sanctions apply to the service either way. Review the worksheet again after any crypto change, new product, or AI or compute feature, and at least every 12 months.

**4. Block prohibited destinations.**
- Block by geo-IP at sign-up and login, and check the billing-address and card-issuer country, for comprehensively sanctioned countries and regions. Today that means Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Crimea, and the so-called DNR and LNR regions of Ukraine. Syria's status changed in 2025, so verify the current OFAC and BIS position.
- Russia and Belarus: OFAC and BIS restrict many software and IT services, for example through OFAC's determinations on IT consultancy and on enterprise management and design software. Take on no Russian or Belarusian customer without the Compliance Lead's sign-off.
- Log blocked attempts instead of dropping them silently.

**5. Screen every party.**
- **When:** before quote acceptance or self-serve activation, when billing details or ownership change, and before each renewal.
- **Who:** the customer, the billing entity, the payer, any reseller, and the end customer behind a reseller.
- **Against:** the Consolidated Screening List (trade.gov) and OFAC's SDN list, plus the EU and UK lists where we sell. Confirm every hit on the source list.
- **Ownership:** for enterprise and reseller deals, identify the owners and apply OFAC's 50 Percent Rule. An entity owned 50% or more in total by blocked persons is blocked even if it is not listed. BIS published an affiliates rule in September 2025 and suspended it for one year in November 2025. Check whether it is back in force.
- Rescreen the whole customer base automatically whenever a list is updated.

**6. Holds.** A potential match, an unresolved red flag or an open licensing question puts the account on HOLD. Nothing is activated, provisioned, downloaded, renewed, charged or supported until the Compliance Lead decides. For false positives, record the identifiers that show they are a different party. If the match to an SDN or blocked entity is confirmed, do not refund or return any money, and escalate to counsel the same day. OFAC blocking reports are due within 10 business days.

**7. Red flags (escalate the same day).** Watch for:
- logins, VPN exits, cards or banks tied to embargoed regions
- a reseller that won't name its end users
- vague answers about end use or ownership
- requests to change names on invoices
- military, nuclear, missile or advanced-chip end uses
- ownership hidden behind holding companies
- a customer asking how to get around our block

Never coach a customer through screening, and never help anyone get around a control.

**8. Technology releases.** Before a foreign-national employee or contractor (offshore developers included) gets access to controlled source code or technology, the Compliance Lead records its classification and whether a license is needed. Most mass-market SaaS code will need no license, but write that down. Collect only the nationality data this check needs, with input from employment counsel. Check license exceptions before staff travel abroad with company laptops.

**9. Records.** Keep these in [system]: classifications, screening results with list dates, adjudications, holds, blocked attempts and licenses. Retain them for at least 5 years for the EAR (15 CFR Part 762) and 10 years for OFAC-related records. Verify the 10-year period, which was extended after the 2024 change to the sanctions statute of limitations.

**10. Training and audit.** Give role-based training to Sales, Support, Finance, Engineering and People at onboarding and every year. Once a year, test a sample of 25 transactions end to end and review the screening tool's tuning and false-positive rate. Update this procedure within 30 days of any relevant rule change.

**11. Possible violation.** Stop the activity, preserve the records, and notify the Compliance Lead and counsel the same day. Counsel decides whether to make a voluntary self-disclosure (BIS under 15 CFR 764.5; OFAC under its Enforcement Guidelines).

Approved: ________ (CEO)   Date: ________

## MEMORANDUM: Privileged and Confidential, Prepared at the Direction of Counsel

*Send this through counsel so privilege can attach. Do not forward it outside this list.*

**To:** CEO, CFO, General Counsel, outside export-control counsel
**From:** Export Compliance
**Date:** [date]
**Re:** Eight months of service to a customer 55% owned by an SDN

I'm not a lawyer or our empowered official. This memo sets out what we know, what we are doing today, and the decisions counsel needs to make. The rules cited are as of October 2026. Verify each one against OFAC's website and the eCFR.

### 1. Bottom line
If the facts hold, [Customer] is a blocked person under OFAC's 50 Percent Rule. Any entity owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, in the aggregate, by blocked persons is itself blocked, whether or not it is on the SDN list. Without OFAC authorization, US persons may not provide it services, accept its payments, or otherwise deal in its property. Eight months of service and payments are likely apparent violations. Civil liability does not depend on whether we knew. Our job now is to stop the ongoing conduct, preserve the evidence, and get counsel a complete file quickly, because the disclosure decision depends on timing.

### 2. Today: the account is on HOLD
1. **Suspend service.** Disable logins, API keys, integrations and support. Do not delete the account or its data.
2. **Freeze the money.** Cancel auto-renewals and scheduled charges, and stop collections. Do not refund, credit or return anything, because returning funds is itself a prohibited transfer. Hold any incoming payment until counsel decides whether it goes into a blocked account.
3. **Preserve records.** Put a legal hold on contracts, order forms, invoices, payment records, screening logs, usage and access logs, email and Slack.
4. **Control communications.** Nothing goes to the customer except a neutral notice that counsel approves. No one suggests restructuring, paying through another party, or any other way around the block.
5. **Keep it need-to-know** inside the company.

### 3. Verify the facts (target: 48 hours)
- **Ownership:** Get the source documents for the 55%. Is it direct or indirect, and when did it reach 50%? Do any other blocked owners hold stakes that add to it? If the stake is really below 50%, the rule may not apply. Large blocked ownership or control is still a red flag, and service stays suspended until counsel decides.
- **Listing:** Confirm the parent's SDN entry, program tags and designation date in OFAC's Sanctions List Search. If it was designated after we onboarded the customer, record that, and check whether a wind-down general license applied.
- **Other regimes:** Check the Entity List and the EU and UK lists if any of our entities or the customer's operations touch those regimes. If the customer downloaded software from us, that is also an EAR question.
- **Scope:** List every invoice and payment (date, amount, paying bank), the services we delivered, and where the customer's users were.
- **Related parties:** Rescreen our whole customer base for other affiliates of the parent.
- **Root cause:** Did we screen at onboarding? By name only? Did we rescreen after the designation?

### 4. OFAC reporting (counsel to confirm)
- Report blocked property within 10 business days (31 CFR 501.603), and include it in the annual report of blocked property (status as of June 30, due September 30).
- Report any payment we reject within 10 business days (31 CFR 501.604).

### 5. Decisions for counsel
- **Voluntary self-disclosure.** Under OFAC's Enforcement Guidelines (31 CFR Part 501, Appendix A), a qualifying disclosure generally halves the base penalty. It usually does not qualify if OFAC has already learned of the conduct some other way, such as a bank's blocking or reject report.
- **Past receipts.** Should amounts we have already collected be placed in a blocked account?
- **Licensing.** Should we seek a specific license to wind down, return the customer's data, or settle amounts owed? Assume we cannot return the data without authorization.
- **Exposure.** Under IEEPA, a civil penalty is the greater of an inflation-adjusted maximum per violation or twice the transaction value (verify the current figure). The statute of limitations has been 10 years since the 2024 amendment.
- **Non-US exposure.** Do any EU or UK obligations apply because one of our non-US entities was involved?

### 6. Corrective actions (30 days)
- Research ownership and apply the 50% rule to enterprise and reseller customers at onboarding.
- Rescreen the full customer base automatically on every list update.
- Connect holds to billing and provisioning so a match actually stops service.
- Keep an adjudication log that records list dates.
- Train Sales, Finance and Support.
- Write up the root cause and keep evidence of the fixes, which OFAC weighs as mitigating factors.

### 7. Owners
| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Suspend service, freeze billing | Engineering lead, Controller | Today |
| Legal hold | General Counsel | Today |
| Fact file (section 3) | Export Compliance | 48 hours |
| Blocking report | Counsel | Within 10 business days |
| Disclosure decision | Counsel, CEO | Once the fact file is done |
| Corrective actions | Export Compliance | 30 days |
